--- title: "Finding the parameters" description: "Linear regression's parameters come from a formula in one step; almost every other model has to search for them, and a search can go wrong in ways a formula cannot." order: 2 categories: [optimisation] --- ## Solved in one step or found by searching [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) gave each fit a number to make as small as possible. This page shows the two ways a model finds the parameter values that do it. Linear regression has a formula that gives them exactly, in one step. Every other model in [Supervised learning](../03-supervised-learning/index.qmd) has to search for them, and a search can stop too early or end in a different place on another run. Knowing which kind of model you have tells you which of those checks it needs. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Parameters and hyperparameters A **parameter** is a number the fit chooses from the data: a slope in a regression, or the value a decision tree splits at. You do not set these. A **hyperparameter** is a number you set before fitting, which controls the fit: the depth of a tree, or the number of trees in a forest. The fit cannot choose it, because its job is to limit what the fit may do. [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd) chose the depth by trying several on the validation sites; [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) returns to this. ::: {.callout-note} ## "Parameter" means different things in different fields In this course a parameter is always a number the fit estimates from the data. Marine science often uses the word differently, so check which meaning a paper or a help page has in mind. - **Oceanography and water-quality monitoring** call the measured variables parameters: temperature, salinity, oxygen and nutrients are "hydrographic parameters". In this course those are [inputs](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) or the outcome, never parameters. - **Population and stock-assessment models** call any constant in the model a parameter, including ones fixed from the literature, such as natural mortality, rather than estimated from the data at hand. - **Statistics** reserves the word for a property of the population, such as the true mean, and calls the fitted value its estimate. - **scikit-learn** calls the settings you pass to a model its parameters, so what this course calls hyperparameters come back from `get_params()`. The values it learns end in an underscore, as in `coef_`. ::: ## The objective as a landscape For a straight line, the objective depends on two parameters, the intercept and the slope. Draw it as a map, with the two parameters as the axes and the objective as the height, and fitting means finding the lowest point. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() d <- survey |> select(abundance, chlorophyll_mg_m3) |> drop_na() grid <- expand_grid( intercept = seq(-2, 6, length.out = 120), slope = seq(-1, 3, length.out = 120) ) |> mutate(mse = map2_dbl( intercept, slope, \(a, b) mean((d$abundance - (a + b * d$chlorophyll_mg_m3))^2) )) best <- coef(lm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3, data = d)) ggplot(grid, aes(intercept, slope, fill = mse)) + geom_raster() + geom_contour(aes(z = mse), colour = "white", alpha = 0.35, bins = 14) + annotate("point", x = best[1], y = best[2], shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.2, colour = "white") + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", trans = "log10") + labs( x = "Intercept", y = "Slope", fill = "Mean squared\nerror (log scale)", title = "The objective for a straight line is a bowl" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The mean squared error of a straight line of abundance against chlorophyll, for every intercept and slope on a grid. Darker is lower. The surface is a long, tilted bowl with one lowest point, marked by the cross at an intercept of 2.36 and a slope of 1.15.](parameter-estimation_files/figure-html/fig-surface-1.png){#fig-surface fig-alt='A filled contour plot with intercept on the horizontal axis from minus two to six and slope on the vertical axis from minus one to three. The colour shades from yellow at the edges to dark blue in a narrow valley running diagonally from upper left to lower right. A white cross marks the single lowest point, at an intercept of 2.36 and a slope of 1.15.' width=1300} ::: ::: ::: The bowl has one lowest point, so every way downhill ends there. It is also long and narrow: along the diagonal valley, a higher intercept with a lower slope fits almost as well, so the data pin down some combinations of the two far better than others. That shape matters on [Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd). There are three ways to find the lowest point, and each kind of model in section 3 uses one of them. ::: {.diagram} ![Linear regression's parameters come from a formula in one step. Poisson and logistic regression search step by step downhill until the objective stops falling. Trees, forests and boosting choose one split at a time and never revisit it.](img/finding-parameters.svg){fig-alt="Three cards. By formula, solved in one step, linear regression: an arrow labelled solve points straight down to the lowest point of a U-shaped objective curve; exact, and the same answer every time. By search, step by step downhill, Poisson and logistic regression: a row of dots from a point marked start steps down the curve, each step shorter, to its lowest point; repeats until the objective stops falling. One split at a time, greedy, trees, forests and boosting: a small tree with its first and second splits filled in; takes the best split now and never goes back to it. A note says a search can stop early or end somewhere else; a formula cannot."} ::: ## Worked example ### Linear regression has a formula For linear regression under squared error, algebra gives the lowest point of the bowl directly: the **normal equations**, solved once. We fit abundance on chlorophyll, depth and temperature this way and compare with `lm()`. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d3 <- survey |> select(abundance, chlorophyll_mg_m3, depth_m, temperature_c) |> drop_na() X <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3) y <- d3$abundance by_formula <- drop(solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y)) by_lm <- coef(lm(abundance ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3)) tibble(term = names(by_lm), `by formula` = by_formula, `by lm()` = by_lm) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | by formula| by lm()| |:-----------------|----------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 5.1170| 5.1170| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.0265| 1.0265| |depth_m | -0.0159| -0.0159| |temperature_c | -0.1313| -0.1313|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() inputs = ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "depth_m", "temperature_c"] d3 = survey[["abundance", *inputs]].dropna() X = sm.add_constant(d3[inputs]).to_numpy() y = d3["abundance"].to_numpy() by_formula = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y) line = LinearRegression().fit(d3[inputs], y) pd.DataFrame({ "term": ["intercept", *inputs], "by formula": by_formula, "by LinearRegression": [line.intercept_, *line.coef_], }).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | by formula | by LinearRegression | |:------------------|-------------:|----------------------:| | intercept | 5.117 | 5.117 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 1.0265 | 1.0265 | | depth_m | -0.0159 | -0.0159 | | temperature_c | -0.1313 | -0.1313 | ::: ::: ::: The two agree: the largest difference is 8e-14, rounding error in the last digits a computer stores. `lm()` solves the same equations by a route that is safer with awkward data. There is no starting value and nothing to converge, so the answer is the same on every run. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it With $X$ the table of inputs (one row per station, plus a column of ones for the intercept), $y$ the observed values and $\beta$ the coefficients, the objective is the sum of squared residuals, $\lVert y - X\beta \rVert^2$. Its lowest point is where its slope in every direction is zero, which gives $$X^\top X \hat\beta = X^\top y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$$ This works because squaring makes the objective a bowl whose lowest point can be solved for. Absolute error has no such formula, which is why [Loss functions](loss-functions.qmd) needed `optim()` for it. ::: ### Logistic regression needs a search [Logistic regression](../03-supervised-learning/logistic-regression.qmd) has no formula for its lowest point, so `glm()` finds it by repeating one step. Each step replaces the objective with a weighted linear regression that matches it near the current coefficients, solves that by formula, and starts again from the answer. We write the steps out, starting from coefficients of zero, and watch the log-likelihood, a measure of fit that [Maximum likelihood](maximum-likelihood.qmd) explains; higher is better. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} d3b <- survey |> select(present, chlorophyll_mg_m3, depth_m, temperature_c) |> drop_na() |> mutate(present = fct_relevel(present, "no")) Xb <- model.matrix(~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3b) yb <- as.numeric(d3b$present == "yes") log_likelihood <- function(b) { eta <- drop(Xb %*% b) sum(yb * eta - log1p(exp(eta))) } b <- rep(0, ncol(Xb)) start <- log_likelihood(b) steps <- map_dfr(1:6, function(k) { eta <- drop(Xb %*% b) p <- plogis(eta) w <- p * (1 - p) z <- eta + (yb - p) / w b <<- drop(solve(t(Xb) %*% (Xb * w), t(Xb) %*% (w * z))) tibble(step = k, log_likelihood = log_likelihood(b), chlorophyll = b[2], depth = b[3], temperature = b[4]) }) steps |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| step| log_likelihood| chlorophyll| depth| temperature| |----:|--------------:|-----------:|--------:|-----------:| | 1| -378.2597| 0.12764| -0.00259| 0.00323| | 2| -373.2629| 0.26844| -0.00342| 0.00185| | 3| -372.8919| 0.33997| -0.00339| -0.00034| | 4| -372.8882| 0.34809| -0.00338| -0.00064| | 5| -372.8882| 0.34817| -0.00338| -0.00064| | 6| -372.8882| 0.34817| -0.00338| -0.00064|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} d3b = survey[["present", *inputs]].dropna() Xb = sm.add_constant(d3b[inputs]).to_numpy() yb = (d3b["present"] == "yes").to_numpy(dtype=float) def log_likelihood(b): eta = Xb @ b return np.sum(yb * eta - np.log1p(np.exp(eta))) b = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1]) start = log_likelihood(b) rows = [] for step in range(1, 7): eta = Xb @ b p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-eta)) w = p * (1 - p) z = eta + (yb - p) / w b = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ (Xb * w[:, None]), Xb.T @ (w * z)) rows.append({"step": step, "log_likelihood": log_likelihood(b), "chlorophyll": b[1], "depth": b[2], "temperature": b[3]}) steps = pd.DataFrame(rows) steps.round(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | step | log_likelihood | chlorophyll | depth | temperature | |-------:|-----------------:|--------------:|---------:|--------------:| | 1 | -378.26 | 0.12764 | -0.00259 | 0.00323 | | 2 | -373.263 | 0.26844 | -0.00342 | 0.00185 | | 3 | -372.892 | 0.33997 | -0.00339 | -0.00034 | | 4 | -372.888 | 0.34809 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | | 5 | -372.888 | 0.34817 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | | 6 | -372.888 | 0.34817 | -0.00338 | -0.00064 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} glm_fit <- glm(present ~ chlorophyll_mg_m3 + depth_m + temperature_c, data = d3b, family = binomial) round(coef(glm_fit), 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> (Intercept) chlorophyll_mg_m3 depth_m temperature_c #> 1.20045 0.34817 -0.00338 -0.00064 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # scikit-learn's LogisticRegression would not match: it adds a penalty by # default (C=1.0), which Priors and ridge regression explains. statsmodels fits # the model as glm() does. glm_fit = sm.GLM(yb, sm.add_constant(d3b[inputs]), family=sm.families.Binomial()).fit() glm_fit.params.round(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> const 1.20045 #> chlorophyll_mg_m3 0.34817 #> depth_m -0.00338 #> temperature_c -0.00064 #> dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: From coefficients of zero, the log-likelihood is −513.6. The first step takes it to −378.3 and the second to −373.3; by step 5 it changes by less than 0.0001, and the coefficients match `glm()`'s. `glm()` reports 5 steps for this model. It stops when a step changes the fit by less than a set tolerance, and calls that converged. ### Trying every combination is out of reach Stepping downhill can look roundabout next to the obvious alternative: try every combination of parameter values on a grid and keep the best. The bowl figure above did exactly that, with 120 values for each of two parameters. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grid_cost <- tibble( parameters = c(2, 4, 10), `grid points at 100 values each` = format(100^parameters, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE) ) grid_cost ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| parameters|grid points at 100 values each | |----------:|:------------------------------| | 2|10,000 | | 4|100,000,000 | | 10|100,000,000,000,000,000,000 |
::: ::: ::: Two parameters make ten thousand combinations, done in a moment. Four, the number in the linear regression above, make a hundred million. Ten make $10^{20}$, which at a billion a second takes about 3,200 years. A search has to use the shape of the objective to go downhill instead of looking everywhere, and [Gradient descent](gradient-descent.qmd) shows the simplest way. ## Trees search one split at a time A decision tree does not walk down an objective at all. At each branch it tries every input and every split value, keeps the one that lowers the squared error most, and moves on without going back. This **greedy** search is fast, but it can miss a better tree whose first split looks worse on its own. Random forests and boosting grow many trees this way, and forests also draw stations and inputs at random, so without a set seed each run gives a slightly different model. A model found by formula has nothing to check about the fit itself. A model found by search can stop before the bottom, stop somewhere other than the bottom, or change from run to run, and none of these shows in its coefficients. [Checking a fit](reading-a-fit.qmd) shows how to spot each one. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Parameters** are chosen by the fit from the data; **hyperparameters**, such as a tree's depth, are set before fitting and limit what the fit may do. - Linear regression under squared error has a formula: one step, exact, and the same on every run. - Poisson and logistic regression search step by step; here logistic regression settled in 5 steps from a start at zero. - Trying every combination is out of reach: ten parameters on a modest grid take $10^{20}$ evaluations. - Trees choose one split at a time and never revisit it; forests and boosting add randomness on top. - A model found by search can fail in ways a formula cannot, so check which kind you have. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Add `salinity_psu` to the formula fit and confirm it still matches `lm()`. 2. Add a copy of depth in other units, `depth_m * 2`, as a fourth input and give it to `lm()`. What does the coefficient table say, and would you have noticed without looking for it? Try the same with `solve()`.
